utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The case be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper, case manager, for the Prosecution. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lukic. Before we turn today to the testimony of our witness, I have to address some administrative matters. Unfortunately, and I have to apologise for this, there are issues to be resolved with priority tomorrow in the morning. And therefore, we have to come back to that what was planned, to have the hearing in the afternoon but in order to have the necessary time, if you don't have severe objections, I would like to start at half past 1.00, and then proceed until 5.00. I can't see any objections at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to put the Trial Chamber on notice, the second witness -- actually both the witness today and the one we anticipate for tomorrow have told us that they have severe problems staying next week, so we hope to complete them both in the next two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I do the same. And as I understood, the decision on the admission of parts of our so-called SK document are not yet right and not yet finished. So in order to not let the witnesses wait too long, we should continue with Dr. Donia next Wednesday. Right? No problem. Fine. And this brings me to another serious question, and I think it's better to address it frankly in the courtroom. This is an International Tribunal, and of course we all are socialised with and under different rules. For example, one Defence counsel normally would never address a judge ex parte, and the other one would be called a bad Defence counsel in his own country having not a good contact to the Judges. Therefore, we have to find a kind of balance, and this balance will be the following: That it's on the record that for the expeditiousness of the proceedings, and when it's really necessary and urgent, the participants of this trial can, of course, contact me directly by phone or coming to my office. There should be no problem at all. I will set the other party on notice of what has happened immediately. This is how things stand. And of course, we need the -- we all need the assistance of legal officers, and therefore it shouldn't be any problem that the legal officers contact the one and the other party separately. I think the main issue is all the parties are informed immediately about what's happened and to avoid any kind of misunderstanding that there is a discussion with one party not with the other and so on. But this should be clear from the beginning. Having said this, I want to inform, especially the Defence, that I got a phone call from Mr. Cayley this morning telling me that for urgent reasons, he would not be able to attend the hearing this afternoon. And he made the suggestion I brought to you to continue with Dr. Donia next witness. Are there any objections to proceed in this way also in the future? I can see this is not the case. In order to prepare for the next days, I had a look on the list given to us from the Office of the Prosecutor yesterday on the envisaged witnesses. The first and main concern is there is a new witness on the list, and number 88 under 65 ter. During the pretrial, we didn't have this witness, and therefore I'm wondering whether this witness can really have a 65 ter number. But this is more a technical question. We know all about -- yeah, we can say -- we can address the name in public? Do you want to have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If no one objects I prefer in private session. To be honest, I'm not quite sure about some matters regarding that, and I think it would be safer in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we continue in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you need some time for the preparation of this technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it's done already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the witness may be called in. Just before the witness comes in, pseudonym was requested. Then the witness should be addressed: "Witness B."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would have -- early in the testimony, have asked the witness a few details regarding his current whereabouts and information such as his date of birth. We could begin in private session, if the Court wants, and I can go through those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections? No objections. When the witness is brought in, immediately after the declaration, we'll go in private session. The witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, sorry, but I have to address you in this impolite manner as Witness B only, but this is a protective measure in your interest. And therefore, please understand this. Could the solemn declaration be taken now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We start in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is confirmed. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you practice a religion now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was a car-body mechanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you active in politics or a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the League of Communists at that time, until, maybe, 1994 approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you as part of your youth perform military service and were you in 1991 a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I served my military term in 1983, and after the army, I was a member of the police reserves in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you remember about that day? Tell us what you recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I remember the 30th of April, Serb forces -- how shall I say it -- took power forcibly in Prijedor, and they took control of the police, the municipal bodies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what your own experience was that day. What do you remember happening, seeing, and hearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I didn't see anything in particular, simply because my house is quite close to the town. In the morning, I was woken up first by my father. And when we went out, he was in a panic, so when we went outside and looked, I saw, because there's a hotel close to my house, I saw that there were Serb flags already flying at the hotel. Then, we turned on the radio, the Radio Prijedor station, and that's when we found out exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you heard that announcement, did you see that day, or in subsequent days, men in uniforms, armed men in uniforms, on the streets of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: From that day on, Prijedor was full of armed people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints near your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The closest checkpoint was on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that bridge be a bridge between your neighbourhood and the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you some questions about what life was like after the takeover. Did the takeover affect your ability to go and move around the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what it was that made you reluctant to move around Prijedor, or unable to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The first step was that we had to show our ID when we crossed the bridge, when we wanted to go into town. That was the only way to get into town for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear announcements on the radio giving orders during this time after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. We heard them. There were plenty of them, and yes, we did hear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what kind of orders were given to the population over the radio.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: First of all, that day, we heard an announcement. It was a decree by the new authorities that they had taken over because the old authorities were not functioning. It couldn't go on any more like that. And more or less, the proclamation was something to that effect, that they had taken over power in order to have a better life in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they had taken over power", was it identified who was now the power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it clear in these orders who among the -- when you say the Serb authorities, was there an institution or body that was named as the supreme authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, at that time there was already talk about a Crisis Staff. I know that the Crisis Staff took power. That's what they started to call themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a curfew ordered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any orders for the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, we did hear about that. But I don't know when. In any case, it was after the 30th of April when the proclamation started. And one of those proclamations was to surrender the weapons. But I don't know how long it was after this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall these orders for the surrender of weapons? Were they directed to all the citizens of Prijedor or were they directed to particular citizens or particular areas? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It basically was for all citizens of Prijedor, non-Serb citizens, meaning Muslims, Croats, and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the orders for surrender directed to the entire municipality, or were they directed to particular neighbourhoods, over the course of various periods of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the beginning -- well, this applied to the territory of the entire municipality. Later, the proclamations applied to certain parts or certain areas of the town and various units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything on the media, the radio- or I don't know if you were able to watch TV or not- anything regarding that you considered propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: From that day on, everything was propaganda, both on the radio and on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Judges some examples of things you recall hearing that you considered were inflammatory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, for example, they used terms such as "mujahedin," "Ustashas," and other derogative names. They didn't call us any more by our proper names; they called us Green Berets and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, what did you do? Did you have a weapon as a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with your weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I returned it to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were a Serb at that time living in Prijedor and listening to go the media that was going on at that time, how would you have felt about your non-Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, after all that I had seen on TV before and after the camp, at that time I wasn't able to watch television and listen to the radio. After all of my troubles, perhaps if I had been a Serb and had seen a Croat or a Muslim on the street, I would have shot him, too. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that based upon the propaganda that was on the media at that time -- that was in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you home that morning, and if so, can you tell us what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, people used different names to describe it, but it was the Muslim attack on Prijedor, a group of armed Muslims and Croats on that day attacked Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your experience? What did you see, hear, and experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was woken up very early in the morning by blasts, explosions. We got up. And I saw that the explosions were coming from the direction of the town. And close to the hotel, I could see that after the explosion, I could see black smoke rising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting for some period of time that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, you could hear shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where you lived, were you able to see Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. It was right across the River Sana, and I could see it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the attack was over, did you hear any announcements on the radio regarding anyone marking their house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. That day, since the only sort of -- source of information, the only way we could find out approximately what was going on was to listen to Radio Prijedor, because we couldn't listen to anything else. So that day, in the course of that day, there was an order that all non-Serbs had to put up white flags on their houses. And this is what I also did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it explained where you got a white flag? What did people use for a white flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Anything white from the house, a sheet, any fabric, any object from the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did life change after the Muslim attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes, drastically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what life was like living in Prijedor, after that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That day, the concentration camps were opened. Already on that day, certain parts of town had all the men -- all the male population from those parts of town transferred to the Omarska camp. My wife's brother also was taken away. So after that day, there were daily arrests and people were being taken to camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Stari Grad? You mentioned you can see Stari Grad from your house. Did you see any damage to Stari Grad after that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That same day, I saw one of the first buildings to burn, the one that you could see most clearly. And that was the old mosque in the Stari Grad, in the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're going to come to some of your experiences in the camps. Did you return, though, to your house near Stari Grad before leaving Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I was released from the camp, and I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you see Stari Grad, in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I saw the area where Stari Grad was, because Stari Grad wasn't there any more. It was the site of it, but now it was a green -- a grassy area, completely cleared, no buildings. And in the middle, there was only one restaurant which was there before the war. It was called Lovac, "the hunter," and it was the property of the hunters' association, hunting society, in Prijedor. And then a little bit further away from the Lovac, there was one small house. So these were the only two buildings standing in the Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was living in that house in August of 1992, the ethnicity of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Until August 1992, it was the property of a Muslim man, that house that remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Not far from that house, there was another house, and I think that that was the only Serb who was living in Stari Grad. And I heard -- I didn't see it myself -- that he wouldn't let them demolish that house because he demolished his own house because this other house was in a better condition. So he moved into that other house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned people being arrested and taken to Omarska and Keraterm. When do you recall first hearing about the Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Practically that same day. We heard about it very quickly, that people were taken away. We heard that on that same day. And then shortly after we found out where they were, at which location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident that happened at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hambarine. What did you recall hearing on the radio about the incident at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I heard that there was an incident at Hambarine at a checkpoint and that three or four Serb soldiers were killed there. And after that, again, we heard an ultimatum over Radio Prijedor that the population of Hambarine had to hand over a certain person because of that incident, as the main culprit for that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time did you go to an area near Hambarine, another village in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, I went to Rizvanovici, which is more or less in the same position. It's a village close to Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Rizvanovici and Hambarine constitute two of about four Muslim villages that were known in this general area as the "Brdo" area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Rizvanovici, what did you hear after going there? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I heard -- I'm sorry, you mean did I hear how the incident came about or...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's go -- were you aware of an attack? Tell us about the attack.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: When I went up there, I heard from the local population how this incident happened. There was a checkpoint set up there by Muslims. Since the Prijedor-Ljubija Road passed through Hambarine, so there were always unfamiliar armed people in vehicles passing through. And since they simply felt that this wasn't all right, they began to check the vehicles that were passing through there. And at one such check, they say that there were -- they said that there were five armed Serb soldiers in one vehicle. And when they wanted to check their IDs, the Serbs wouldn't allow that, and they started firing from the vehicle. They returned fire, and we heard information that four were killed and one person was captured there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the response of the authorities after that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, they immediately demanded that a certain man be handed over, as I've already said. And that the population of Hambarine -- in fact, the population of the entire Brdo -- surrender whatever weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the person that they demanded surrender is Mr. Aliskovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Aliskovic, yes. The first name is Aziz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people in the Brdo region surrender their weapons, any or all of the people surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Not that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Then Serb forces started shelling Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find out about the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, I was up there myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There was not much you could see, but shells were falling all around us. We were hiding in a basement, and we could hear the shells. We saw a couple of locations where they fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after the -- when the shelling slowed down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the intervals between rounds of shelling, we found cases and empty shell cartridges scattered about the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell from -- did you have any idea what kind of weapons were being used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, from our earlier experience from the JNA, and there were several of us who had done our military duty, we concluded that those were tanks and mortars doing the shelling, although we couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, did you go back to your neighbourhood near Prijedor town, through Biscani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go up to -- first of all, did you take part in any of the fighting or any fighting in the Brdo area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any militia or armed resistance group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you leave your neighbourhood and go to Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Simply because my house was surrounded by Serb homes, and my neighbours were Serbs. And I thought I would feel more comfortable and safer up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have family in Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, because that's the place where we originally come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, then, that Hambarine was in the end of April -- excuse me, around the end of May, around the 25th of May, and you were in your neighbourhood in Prijedor town until the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, later when I returned from Rizvanovici, I was at home all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you stay at home all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Because I didn't know where to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you afraid to travel around Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was impossible to travel anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any houses searched before your arrest? Before the day of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about on the day of your arrest? Tell us what happened that day. And again, this is the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, that morning when we woke up, our street was already encircled by armed men from Tukovi. The people from Tukovi were our neighbours, and they had already encircled our street. And from the direction of Prijedor, military police were walking along the streets, searching our houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your Serb neighbours doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They surrounded our street, probably to prevent us from running away through our backyards and fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the houses searched thoroughly, if you could tell? Or what actually happened in the search, if you were able to observe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, I was able to observe the search of my own home. It was nothing special. They didn't search it very thoroughly. They just walked in, looked inside the closets, and then walked out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your family that day? Were you all kept together, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: After they had searched the houses and went on to continue searching the houses of our neighbours, they told all of us to get out. They allowed my father to stay in, while myself and my two brothers were told to get out into the road and wait there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other men with you, and approximately how many were there with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In total, there were 20 to 25 men who were found at home that day in our street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, Stipo Gavranovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who beat him, and can you describe briefly the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: First they brought all the people from our neighbourhood to the intersection of Djure Djakovica and another street. We were waiting for something. We didn't know what. And all around us were the mil -- it was the military police. Our neighbours were no longer there. And close to the place where we were sitting, some bricks and pallets were lying. And Stipo sat down on to one of those bricks. And then one military policeman started to beat him. And even outside his own house earlier on, he was also beaten, but I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and the other men taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. After a rather long wait, a bus came. We were loaded on to that bus and transported to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the bus as coming from a public -- excuse me, coming from a company in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. The bus belonged to the Autotransport company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm coming now to the experience in the camp. If you would like to take a break, this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The trial stays adjourned. We resume 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us first of all come back to the motion of the Defence. I have to announce the following decision of the Chamber: The Defence's motion on providing all former transcripts of a witness is dismissed. First of all, to a certain extent, it's to apply Rule 66 to 68 correspondingly. And the Trial Chamber believes that there is nothing special with former transcripts opposed, for example, to other former statements of a person, be it in public or not public. We have to decide on the individual criminal responsibility of Dr. Stakic on the basis and in the limits of the fourth [Realtime transcript read in error"first"] amended indictment. As it is true for all other statements, the special relevance for the case before us must be demonstrated, also when it's on the question of former transcripts. Of course, additionally, it has to be pointed out that there are two exceptions: One, if one party wanted to come back and make reference of a former transcript, this transcript has to be made available for the other party and the Bench seven days prior to the day of the hearing of the witness. And additionally, it remains the duty of the Office of the Prosecutor, whenever they identify exculpatory material in a former transcript, this has to be disclosed in the same way to the Defence and to the Bench. May I ask whether there is already an opinion of the Defence on the question of lineup of the envisaged witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is an opinion. And our opinion is that respectfully we would ask that the Court order a lineup for the particular witness that the Office of the Prosecution wishes to call, I believe, tomorrow. So we would ask that that lineup proceed -- next Friday, I'm sorry. And that would be Witness under 65 ter Number 47, in the calling order, Number 7, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this statement. We will make a decision tomorrow early that we can ask the Office of the Prosecutor to provide the necessary -- let me just check what is laid down here. For the record, please, probably I was misunderstood. At 16.20.57, it's not the first but the fourth amended indictment. Could that please be corrected. Thank you. Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just comment on the lineup, Your Honour, I don't have any experience in conducting a lineup here, so I'm using, I'm relying somewhat on my knowledge of my prior jurisdiction, but also my understanding of the relationship between the Detention Unit and the Office of the Prosecutor. The Detention Unit is clearly separate and does not come under the authority of the Office of the Prosecutor. The Office of the Prosecutor is prepared to provide the witness and ensure that he is transported to the lineup, if the Court orders a lineup. But the physical arrangements, I think would have to be done by the Detention Unit including finding the other individuals to stand in the lineup. I don't think the Defence would care for us to select them. They should be selected if the Court orders it by the Detention Unit. I know it's going to be a very difficult logistical operation. The witness will be here by Wednesday morning, so we can do it any time from Wednesday or Thursday, if that's possible, day, morning, or night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for those comments. I believe we can proceed now hearing Witness B. May Witness B be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps -- I don't know if Your Honour wants me to speak now or later, but I would like to clarify that we indicated this issue was coming up for the Court's benefit because the Court had identified the issue in pretrial. It's not our opinion that a lineup will be particularly useful. We believe this witness is a recognition witness who has indicated he knows -- knew Dr. Stakic before. I do not have information about whether he has seen pictures of him since his arrest. We also indicated in pretrial our position regarding the change in appearance. But I put before the Chamber the issue that there would be a possible identification of Dr. Stakic in the camp by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Witness B. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, can you describe what you saw when the buses arrived at the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: When we arrived at Keraterm, there was nobody outside in the compound. And since the bus had stopped and we had got out and were lined up, we were able to see that there were people inside the rooms on the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many rooms were there in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There were four rooms in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Judges what that camp looked like and what the rooms were like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, it used to be a big company, a big factory. And in the back where the camp was set up, there were premises which had been used for storage before the war. And the rooms were called 1, 2, and 3. And the numbers went from the Prijedor-Banja Luka Road. Across the road was Room Number 1, followed by Rooms 2, 3, and 4. The biggest was Room Number 2. And the smallest was Number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were in the Keraterm camp at one time, would you estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, at one point, in end June, we were ordered to make a list of prisoners per room, including name, surname, father's name, and occupation. And according to that list, only in our room, Number 1, there were about 320 persons, prisoners, while Room Number 2 contained 450. In late July, that number had considerably grown. As for Rooms Number 3 and 4, I couldn't tell how many people there were at that moment, but they were full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based upon the size of those rooms in comparisons to Rooms 1 and 2 where you said there were approximately 750 in total in Rooms 1 and 2, how many would you estimate there would be in the camp in total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At that time, in late June, there were over 1200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did prisoners arrive at the camp often? Would you say it was on a weekly basis, a daily basis, or did they just come a few times while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There was no rule governing new arrivals. People were brought in every day in smaller or greater numbers. But every day, somebody would be brought in. Somebody would be taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's clear, you were brought to the camp on June 18th. What day did you leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Around the 5th of August. I think it was the 5th of August when we got out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the day the camp was closed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the guards in the camp? Could you tell whether they were police or army, and did you recognise any of them? Without naming them, did you recognise any of them from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I knew many people. And the force in question was the reserve police. Whether they belonged to Prijedor or Cirkin Polje or some other municipality, I don't know. All I know is they were reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Cirkin Polje. Was Cirkin Polje an area or a settlement within Prijedor municipality, or was that a separate municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, that belonged to the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you don't know which particular police station within the municipality they belonged to, but they were part of the Prijedor municipal reserve police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any army around the camp that you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. On the other side of Keraterm, there were offices of the military police. They could be seen frequently in the vicinity of the camp. And the largest force that came to reinforce the guards' detail was from the Territorial Defence, to reinforce, as I said, the team of guards. But they came only to be there during the day and returned home every evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- I forget your exact words, but you talked about a military headquarters. Was that on the other side of the road directly across from the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That was on the other side of the Prijedor-Banja Luka Road, not within the perimeter. They were housed on the premises of the Kozara Putevi company. It was some sort of military headquarters. I don't know what units were situated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, then, is that different from the military police headquarters you talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. The military police were within the perimeter of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the Judges the conditions that the prisoners lived in in the Keraterm camp. First, can you describe the space that you had to live and sleep in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was a large storage room. We slept on pallets normally used for the transport of goods. Those are wooden pallets where goods lie before being loaded by forklifts onto trucks. Many people slept on bare concrete. And, at the time when I arrived at the camp, the camp was already well filled, so that we were placed near the door which had bars on it like a prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much space did you have between you and the persons lying next to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There was no space in between people. People lay directly next to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, did it become necessary where you were sleeping for people to put parts of their bodies on top of the parts of the bodies of the person next to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically in the spot where I slept, I have to say that we lay lined as sardines with our heads next to the wall. And the inmates who came later also slept very close to us, but their heads were next to the bars. So in the evening, when we lay down to sleep, four or five of us had our legs almost intermingled, intercrossed, forming a net. And all night, we shifted. The person who had his legs under the legs of another person lay like that as long as he could stand it, and then they would sort of change places. He would put his legs on top of the other person's legs, because there was no other way you could take it all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, could you tell us how many people in your room approximately? You said you counted once.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was in June that we made those lists. In fact, in late June, the number was 320 at the time, and it continued growing steadily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the dimensions of this room, could you give us an idea so we can imagine the size of the room that you were in? Was it as big as this room, bigger, or smaller? Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was larger than this, but not much larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the food that you received. How many meals a day did you receive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We got one meal per day, and I don't think it's really necessary to describe it, because there isn't much to describe. Two thin slices of bread and some sort of stew, mainly water with cabbage and perhaps a couple of potatoes in it. But we didn't get even that every day. There were days, when for reasons we ignored, the stew was never distributed, and all we got were the slices of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the families of prisoners bring food to the camp for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, yes, our families tried every day to get some food through to us, also some clothes. But they rarely succeeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know that people's families were trying to bring food and other goods to prisoners that they did not receive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, I saw it. You could see it. When they came, our fathers, mothers, sisters, they had to pass by the camp. They had to walk along. And when we see them with bags containing food in their hand and return 20 minutes later empty-handed, it means that the food was taken from them somewhere at the gate. And then we would wait to see if it would come through to us. And sometimes they returned home carrying their bags with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how often would the prisoners receive the bags of food and other goods left by their families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, they got it very rarely. As for myself, I got food from my family and from -- from my family only twice. I mean, myself and the other members of my family who were inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how often your family tried to bring food or other clothes or goods for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Almost every day, someone would come. They would try every day, and sometimes they would turn them back from the bridge. Sometimes they weren't even able to cross the bridge and enter town. But practically every day, somebody tried to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the prisoners in the camp interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The usual police questions, nothing special. "Are you a member of the party?" "Do you have weapons?" "Who is selling weapons?" So at that time, these questions were quite usual. "Did you go out to vote?" "Who did you vote for?" And so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone beaten in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the camp? Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This would happen every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it happen during the day, at night, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the beginning, in the month of June and partly in July, it was mostly at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about later, just before the camp was closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: From approximately the 20th of July, when the people from Brdo came, then there were no rules. People were beaten night and day then. Night and day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people that were beating the prisoners? Were they guards or other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There were no rules there. Mostly the guards, but anybody could come into the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see people in military uniforms come into the camp and beat people, army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see civilians come into the camp, people in civilian clothes, and beat and kill people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people in your room beaten inside the room or were they called out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, there was no beating inside the room, because the guards didn't enter the rooms, except for individuals. But they would call people out, and the person who was called out had to go out of the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people get called out of the room and not return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did that happen in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This didn't happen very often in my room. For those who were called out, not to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have information about other rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Because after the people were called out at night, then they would open the door for us in the morning, for us to go to the toilet. And the night before, if people were called out and when we would hear this and the beatings, then those who would not come back to the rooms, meaning those who were killed, were left approximately towards Room Number 4, next to a container. And then vehicles would come. In the beginning, this was some kind of utility services vehicle that would come, and that vehicle would take away those bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "a utility service vehicle", can you describe it or tell us a little bit more about it? Was this something that was part of the municipal service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was a vehicle that was used to transport or for funeral services, to transport bodies, even before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us any estimate of how many bodies you, yourself, saw, how many corpses, at the Keraterm camp? And right now I'm not talking about Room 3 incident, which we'll come to later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Besides those killed in Room 3, I saw at least five or six more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone named Dzemal Mesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. That man died next to me in my cell, because he used to sleep close to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges what happened the night that this man died.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: One of the guards called out "Dzemal Mesic" and told him to come outside. And he did. And then after a certain amount of time -- and in the meantime, we heard blows. And then after a certain amount of time, he was brought back to the cell. Those who were closest to the door placed him in the place where he was usually lying down. And then very shortly afterwards, maybe after a couple of minutes, he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the time that someone named Suad Halvadzic was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That was a night or two after Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides being beaten, did anything else happen to his body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. A part of his ear was ripped off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to move quickly so we can finish your testimony. But I want to ask you, in the camp, were there women that you saw in the Keraterm camp? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There were no women except -- well, women did come. They would leave women at the camp, those who were waiting for some transport or vehicles to transfer them to Omarska. Two women even spent the night in our cell. But as a rule, they didn't stay there for long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there minors, people under 18 or even under -- well, people under 18, minors, in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. I even met a boy. He introduced himself to us. And through our conversation, he said that in -- in the conversation, he said that he was 14 years old. You could see that he was a child, but we were really amazed that -- when we heard that he was so young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any people that were older, past the normal retirement age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, there were older people there, much older than retired people, because I think you could go and retire after -- once you were 60. But there were people who were much older than that. There was even a person who we thought perhaps was even over 70 years old. This was an old man from Kozarac. He wasn't very tall, but he was quite fit. And you could see that he was healthy. He was alert. And every morning, when we would get up, he would do some exercises, which we found a little silly at that time, because he was the only one who did that. But he happened to be the oldest amongst us. So while we were talking to him, he even told us that he was in Hitler's camp. That's what he told us. He said, "I was in Hitler's camp, too, during World War II. So then we asked him: "Which one is worse?" And he laughed and he said, "This one is a hundred times worse." Because he was in Germany in a labour camp. And he said, "Nobody beat me. I had food to eat. I had my own bed." So he said that this one was much, much worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the night of the Room 3 incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges about what had happened in the day or two before that incident that led up to that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: One day the guards in the camp, in our camp, completely emptied Room Number 3 where, up until that time, they had mostly people from Kozarac in that cell. They emptied it and they allocated the people from Kozarac to the other three cells. We didn't know what was going on. But after a couple of hours, we saw that buses were coming with new people. And these were the people from Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these prisoners put into Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. They were all put in Room 3, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately what time -- what the date was approximately when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was approximately the 20th or the 21st of July when the first started to arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these prisoners from the Brdo area treated differently; and if so, describe how they were treated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, they were treated very differently. The first few days - I don't know how many days - they didn't receive any food. And then mostly all of the beatings and the abuse was concentrated in their room, so that the other rooms were spared somewhat from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the night that so many men were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That day, sometime in the afternoon -- since we didn't have watches, nobody had a watch because we were robbed before that, so the only way we could orient ourselves was by the sun. So sometime in the afternoon, a large group of soldiers entered the camp, which was not usual for that time. And even if they did enter the camp, there wouldn't be so many of them. They immediately picked out people from Room 3 for themselves and they lined them up on the grassy area in front of Rooms Number 1 and 2 and started to beat them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the men were beaten, were they returned to the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know that, because we were ordered to turn our backs to the door, so that we were able to just see a little bit. So that I don't know what happened to those people when they were returned to the rooms. I don't know when they returned to the rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a day where you saw soldiers with a machine-gun in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That was that day, that day that we're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the course of that day, a table was placed in front of Room Number 3. It looked like a school desk. And a little bit later, we saw that a machine-gun was placed on that desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That night, what happened that you could hear or see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I didn't see anything that night. We only heard things. First we heard the inmates from Room Number 3. We heard some strange sounds, nothing audible, nothing intelligible. We just heard some strange sounds, as if they were all speaking at the same time, or trying to say something. That's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did you hear? Tell us what happened that night that you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We heard the moans, those sounds, from Room Number 3. I heard the shift commander, Kole, he was there. We heard him -- I heard him asking or begging for something, requesting something from those people who had come, pleading with the people who had come to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you remember hearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I remember that he said something to the effect: "Don't touch Rooms Number 1 and 2."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some time, did you hear gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. After that, it wasn't that we heard shots. We heard bursts of fire from several weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your room in relation to Room 3? Can you give us an idea of how far away you were and how it was arranged between you, where the machine-gun was, and where Room 3 was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Room Number 3 was in the same line. My room was Number 1, then Number 2, and then Number 3. The machine-gun was placed in front of Room Number 3, and it was at that moment, perhaps 30 metres away from me. Not more. Maybe not even that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the bursts of gunfire go on for? Can you describe what you heard that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It went on for a long time. Well, they were repeated. First we would hear bursts of fire. Then it would stop for a little bit. Then we would hear individual shots. Then again, there would be a lull. Then again we would hear bursts of fire. So I couldn't really estimate how long this took. According to our estimate, from the moment the shooting began until all of the shooting stopped, according to our estimate, it went for about two hours, although...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the people in your room doing when the shooting was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Nothing. We were silent, and we were lying down, and waiting to see if our turn would come as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone -- did any bullets pass into your room to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. A man in my room was wounded, and in Room Number 2, one man was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the next morning? What did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The next morning, that morning, they didn't let us go to the toilet at all, because you could see that there were a lot of bodies in the compound in front of Room Number 3. So that they didn't allow us to go out anywhere. After that, a truck came. First, a small truck came from the local utility company to pick up the dead and then, the guards really laughed because they had sent them this vehicle, and there was so many bodies. It was a small truck that you couldn't even load ten people on to. So then this small truck went back, and a trailer truck entered the Keraterm compound. It was parked roughly near Rooms 1 and 2, and then the bodies began to be loaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was loading the bodies on to the trailer truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I know one man. The people from Room Number 3 were supposed to do the loading. I don't know why they couldn't do it. Probably some of them were quite tortured. Some of them were sick. And they asked: "Is anybody willing to volunteer to do this, people who are not horrified or afraid of such things? So who is willing to come and help us with the loading?" And they promised that those who helped would be returned to the cells. And then one man from my room volunteered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: After that, all the dead were loaded, all the wounded were also loaded, all those who were wounded that night. And also, 15 fit, healthy men, were also put on the trucks allegedly for unloading of the bodies since the truck was covered with tarpaulin, the tarpaulin was closed, and the truck left the camp, going in the direction of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to one of the people that had loaded the bodies on to the trailer truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, with the man who volunteered, and they really did return him to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how many bodies he had loaded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think that there was talk about 128 dead bodies. We, ourselves, could count about 45 wounded and 15 healthy men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the truck leave the Keraterm camp that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the people, the injured, or the 15 healthy, that you saw get on that truck, did you ever see or hear of them being alive again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident that happened a day or two after the Room 3 shooting involving the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was a day or two later, after the massacre. The men from Room Number 3 were driven out of their room and ordered to line up -- in fact, to lie down on the ground on their stomachs on the turf outside Room Number 3 with their hands behind their necks and sticking their heads as deep down into the grass as they could. The then commander of the camp was there at the time, the warden, holding a rifle in his hand, and he was surrounded by a couple of guards. Those men were told that whoever moved would be finished, gone. The warden of the camp raised his rifle and seemed to be playing with it until he actually fired a shot in the direction of the people lying on the ground. Later on, one of the guards took out his pistol, walked among those people who were lying down, and fired a shot in the direction of somebody's head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see what happened to that person? Did you actually see him being shot in the head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, from that distance, I can say that the guard was right next to the man, so the barrel of his gun must have been no more than 40 centimetres away from the person's head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to -- you were telling us about when the men from Brdo who were brought to the camp in late July were beaten before the massacre. Was there anything else done to those men to humiliate them that you saw? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At one point, I mustered up all my courage to look outside, and I saw people naked from the waist down. And half of them were standing, and half of them were kneeling. And they were positioned in such a way as if engaged in intercourse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that were naked that you saw were the prisoners from Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. All of them were from Room -- from Cell Number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on now to the day that the camp closed. Can you tell us -- before I move on to that, what was the name of the camp commander that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Commander Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the day the camp closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Early that morning, we saw that a large number of buses had arrived outside the Keraterm camp. The commander of the camp came, carrying some papers, and we were told that the people whose names he calls out should come out of the line, one by one, and stand on the tarmac. About 120 people were called out. They were lined up there and put on to two buses which drove away towards Kozarac under escort. Later, when the buses had left, the other buses entered the perimeter of the Keraterm, and all the rest of us were told to get on to the buses and that no one must stay behind. We did so, and we were transferred to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a moment I want to talk about the buses that you talked about in your testimony. You said that when you were arrested that you were taken to the camp by an Autotransport Prijedor bus. You also said that a truck came after the Room 3 massacre and took the bodies away. Do you remember if there were any markings on that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, that truck, too, belonged to the Autotransport company. I know that from the lettering on the truck itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the two buses that came and took away the you said approximately 120 men whose names were called out the day the camp closed. Do you know what kind of buses those were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Those buses were the usual public transport buses in Prijedor. They had some seats, like benches, inside, with more standing than sitting places, and they were normally used for public transport purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Buses that took you and the others whose names were not called to Trnopolje, what kind of buses were those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The same buses of the same class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And jumping ahead to -- I believe you're going to tell us later about being transported on a convoy over Vlasic mountain towards Travnik, what kind of buses were used, and trucks, in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Again, the buses of the Prijedor Autotransport company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On these buses, could you tell if the drivers were the normal drivers that would have been in normal times been driving the buses transporting people within the city or municipality, civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the convoy that took us across Mount Vlasic, the drivers wore civilian clothes. They did not have uniforms. But I don't know whether they were normally employed in the public transport services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So going back to the day the camp closed, you said that 120 or so names were called out. Did you know the names of any of the people who were called out and got on one of those two buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I knew quite a lot of people out of those 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the names now, just at this moment, of people that you remember being called out and getting on one of those two buses the day the camp closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember. Those were my neighbours who had been taken away together with me. Anto Gavranovic, for one. Juro Matanovic. He was one of those who were called out and taken away in those buses. Refik Pelak, Ismet Avdic, Alija Alibegovic, Esad Islamovic, Rasim Music.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear where those buses next went or where they went later that day after leaving Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They drove away in the direction of Kozarac. And when we were transferred to Trnopolje, a certain number of inmates from Omarska joined us in Trnopolje and told us that those people were brought that day to Omarska, spent there only a short while, were again loaded on to buses that same day, and driven away, and they didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear if any of the prisoners from Omarska were put on to the buses during that stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I know only one name but they say that a couple of more people were loaded on to the bus, too. All of those people from Keraterm, plus some people from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of the one person you know from Omarska who was ordered on to the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Dr. Esad Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Esad Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that he had been a doctor for -- in the Seychelles working for an international organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I heard about that later. I didn't know it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the people that you saw having their names called out at Keraterm and getting on those two buses ever seen again alive by you o ever seen again alive to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a place in Sanski Most called -- and forgive my pronunciation -- Hrastova Glavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, some of the people who had been taken away on buses were later found in a place called Hrastova Glavica and identified. Well, if you ask me about the number of bodies identified, I don't know. But a large number of bodies were found, about 145. How many of them were identified, I don't know. I know that some of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. We'll present other evidence regarding that. When you say they were found, do you mean their corpses were found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The corpses were found; in fact, the bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see when these prisoners were called out and put on the bus, who it was that was escorting the prisoners? What kind of people were they? Were they soldiers or police? Did you recognise the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The escort was from the police. I believe it was the reserve police force. They belonged to the Prijedor police force, but they were not active-duty. It was one of the reserve units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for just a question or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Then private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were released from Keraterm or taken away from Keraterm, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: To Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe Trnopolje to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We were unloaded not far from the schooling building in Trnopolje. Close to the school, there was a structure which resembled a small cinema and it had a large yard, a wide perimeter, so we had more space for walking. We were unloaded from the buses there, and we were told to get by as best we could. We were left to our own means and devices, decide ourselves what we would do, where we would sleep. And most of the inmates ended up sleeping under the sky, on the grass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: A lot. Several thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, was life different in the Trnopolje camp from Keraterm? Was there more freedom for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, more freedom. As a rule, food was easier to get. Visits came through more easily. Our fathers, mothers, sisters could reach us and bring us some food; also, we got food from the Serbs once a day. And we had a larger, wider perimeter, inside which we could walk. There were a lot of people from Kozarac, who were there with their families. There were women and children waiting for some convoys or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to Keraterm for a moment, what were the ethnicities of the inmates in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There were Muslims and Croats. There was a pretty large number of Croats, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The same thing, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard people claim that Trnopolje was a refugee centre, and that people were there voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. But that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you free when you were in Trnopolje to -- you and the others who came from Keraterm -- to walk out if you wanted to and go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We could do that, but under certain conditions, which were dictated by the Serbs. I wasn't there long, just four or five days. And I was released to go home after that. Because one of the rules concerning release from the camp was that those who had a formal decision on leaving the autonomous district or region of Krajina, whatever they called it, and to get that decision, you had to sign. And in my case, my wife did it for me. Somebody could do it for you from your family. At any rate, you had to sign that you are waiving all your rights to your own property in favour of that entity, whatever it was called, autonomous region of Krajina. My wife brought this formal decision, this piece of paper, and based on that, I was issued with my release papers which said that I was free to go home. And that meant that I had to take the first convoy out, because I had no longer any property there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to your release papers in a moment. Just a few quick questions about the Trnopolje camp. Were people beaten at the Trnopolje camp, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At Trnopolje, I watched one beating in those few days that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- what actually physically prevented the prisoners from leaving the camp? Was there a wall? Were there guards? What stopped you from just walking out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, first, there was no wire fence or any other fence around the entire camp making a full circle. But there were checkpoints that you had to pass positioned on all routes out of the camp. And if they saw anyone Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. coming towards them in civilian clothes, they would certainly check their papers. So there was absolutely no chance for anyone to escape or to pass through without some formal permit or certificate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good time for a break. And I anticipate 15, 20 minutes left of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned. We resume 6.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May witness be brought in immediately, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just introduce Mr. Bergsmo who is a member of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Welcome aboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, we were talking about your stay and release from the Trnopolje camp. In order to be released from the Trnopolje camp, can you describe what kind of paperwork or what kind of administrative matters you had to take care of, or your family had to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: A little earlier, I was saying that they had to go somewhere. I never asked them or found out. My wife or my father or somebody had to go to the police or to the municipality, but I don't know where, to get this paper signed that all the property we have is being left to some kind of institution or body of theirs, the Serb institution. I don't know what it was called. It's an entity or something like that. I don't know exactly what it was called. And then when they signed it, then they would be allowed to leave the Serb entity. That's when you could be, then, on the basis of that document, issued release papers from Trnopolje. Also, they found out -- I was still at Keraterm. They found out that that was one of the ways that we could be released from the camp. So that's what our family did for all of three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the Judges would be interested if you could tell us what were the other ways you heard an individual could be released from the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That was the way that I got out. There was another way: When two Serbs would come, and they would sign something for a particular Muslim individual, that perhaps they were taking him home. And we also heard, but I don't know if anybody was released in that way, we heard that a person could be released because there was also a Red Cross in Prijedor, that it was possible to leave the camp if you were a blood donor, if a person, perhaps, gave blood a certain number of times before the war, then it was possible to be released in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
