utterances.text: You say that you were released by going through the procedure where you signed away all of your property rights. Once that was done, did you actually receive a certificate at the camp that allowed you to walk out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I didn't sign the document. My wife signed it on my behalf, and then she brought that decision. And based on that decision, they made up my release papers, that I was being released from Trnopolje. And at the same time, it was also a pass for me permitting me to cross all the checkpoints on the way to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you maintain a copy of that release paper, and did you have your wife fax it to my office to my attention the evening of April 23rd, two days ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have that document. I don't want to necessarily have it admitted because it's very short and not translated. But I would like the witness to be able to read and go through the document. Counsel has a copy, and I could also distribute a copy of the actual document to the Court to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness have a copy, please, to refer to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the document before you. Is this a copy or a faxed copy of the released certificate that you obtained at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The writing in the upper right which I believe says Za Koumjian, is that something that your wife wrote on the fax to me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. She wrote that. That is the person that is supposed to receive the paper, the fax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the printing, realising that it's very light, on the upper left, the printed material.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: "Municipal Organisation of the Red Cross of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the document, there's some hand writing in the middle that includes your name in the top line. In the original is there actually some typed material to the left of the handwriting that indicates, for example, name on the top line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It is written: "Receipt," and then below that, there is my personal data, name, last name, date of birth, the town, a number, probably the number of my ID card, my former ID card issued in Prijedor. And below it states: "Trnopolje, the 5th of August, 1992." Then again it states: "Prijedor," my address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Below that material, in the bottom centre there's a stamp. And can you just -- with a cross. Can you read what is stamped in the material next to the cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It states: "The Red Cross of Bosnia and Herzegovina" -- well, the Red Cross of B and H -- "the municipal conference of the Red Cross, Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There appear to be two signatures above the cross. First there's one under your personal data. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I recognise both signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting with the one that's under your personal data, the one on your right, whose name is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The name is Pero Curguz. At that time, he was in charge of the Red Cross office at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name on the left, the signature on the left, again it's left and above the cross, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You can't see the first and last name here, but I know this signature very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It's Slobodan Kuruzovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Slobodan Kuruzovic's job was on the 5th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: He was the commander, the warden, of the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Below the signature of Mr. Curguz, there is some writing, some handwriting. If you can read that, read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. It states as follows: "Released, based on the certificate of departure of AK Krajina, number 03-3-896-413 on the 8th of August, 1992."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And by the way, you said the 8th of August. Is it clear to you what the digit is, 08 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that clear to you, the second 8?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, the 8th. That's the day when I went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but to be complete, can Witness B please explain what is the abbreviation "AK"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's Autonomna ^ Krajina, autonomous region, or -- A is for autonomous, and the other letter, I don't know what it stands for. Or it could be autonomous region, AR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with the document if the Court is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You want to offer this as an exhibit? Evidence, I think, for completeness and, in order, probably later on, to follow what we have done, it would be -- it would make sense in case the Defence wants to come back to this document. I think it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then what would be the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Number S12B [Realtime transcript read in error "S1B"], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S12B [Realtime transcript read in error "S1B"]. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Since we just received the document this afternoon, we would like an opportunity to discuss it, and we would ask that the Court respectfully reserve the right or reserve the ruling on the admissibility of the document until we've had time to consult and determine whether our objection both on authenticity and signatures can be verified. So at this point, to make such an objection may be preliminary, but once again, respectfully, if the Court can reserve the right, understanding that this witness has answered some questions in any event in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's additional item on the agenda for next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were released from Trnopolje and when you went back to your house, was anyone in your house at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, no one except for my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at your house before you left the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I stayed there for about ten days approximately. I don't know exactly. But not long. Maybe about 10 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you leave the region? Describe that process.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Since at that time, after the massacre at Brdo, the entire population had moved away from there, towards Tukovi. So the convoys were going while we were still at the camp, but a lot of people still stayed. And these people were waiting for the Serb authorities to organise a convoy or convoys for them to cross over to Muslim territory. That's how they called it. So while I was at home, I decided to join a convoy like that. So one day in the morning, about ten days after I had arrived home, I could see many trucks and buses going down my street. And we assumed that this was a convoy, that these are trucks which were supposed to take us to Muslim territory somewhere. So we decided to board such a convoy, get on to one of those trucks. It was all very rushed. We made our decision. We took a few things with us, and we went exactly to the place where the trucks and the buses were filling with people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there police at this point, or soldiers, at the point where the convoy was being loaded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. The police was there already, the reserve police was there, when the convoy was being formed. So they were the ones who organised how many people would get on to which truck, how many people would get on to the buses. They were the ones who were doing all of these things. A truck or a bus would come to an open field. Then they would let through a certain number of passengers. Then the truck would leave that place, and an empty one would come in its place. So that all the loading took place in one location. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people boarded that convoy in your estimate? Can you give us an estimation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. Many people, thousands of people, were waiting for convoys. But how many boarded, I don't even know myself how big the convoy was. I don't know the number of vehicles in it. So I couldn't make an estimate. But there was a large number of people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you said, would it be correct for us to understand that more people were waiting than there was room on the convoy? That not everyone was able to find a space on one of the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, a large number of people stayed behind. They didn't all board this convoy. Other convoys were formed after our convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the route that the convoy took briefly? Can you tell us where you went when you left that area in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We passed through Prijedor and set out in the direction of Banja Luka through Kozarac, Omarska, Banja Luka. From Banja Luka, we went to Skender Vakuf. And then from Skender Vakuf onwards. There was the Mount Vlasic. There weren't any inhabited places after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and your family on a bus or a truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We were in a bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you stopped first in Kozarac. Did any other vehicles join your convoy in Kozarac, and did you learn where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, the convoy stopped on the Prijedor-Banja Luka Road approximately -- yeah, at a petrol station in Kozarac. We stopped there. And after a certain amount of time, we were joined by four buses. And then the convoy continued on its way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the people on those buses at any point during the convoy or after you reached your ultimate destination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: For a while, I finished the trip together with them, because at some point, on Mount Vlasic, the bus that I was in broke down. So the passengers from that bus were moved to the other buses and trucks in the convoy. And I got on to one of those buses in which the inmates from Trnopolje already were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the convoy, did anyone ever come on to your bus and rob the passengers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: While I was on the first bus, which broke down, it was stopped, and one of the soldiers who were part of the escort told us some story that we were supposed to pass by Seselj's men, Arkan's man, and such troops. And lest our women be raped and our children killed, we should empty our pockets of all valuables and collect anything worthwhile we had and hand it over to them, so that they could pass it on to those troops as some sort of fee for safe passage. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that came on the bus and collected the valuables, was he a policeman or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was a policeman, one of the policeman from our escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise this person as one of the same policeman you saw escorting the two buses that left Keraterm the day the camp was closed in which all of those who entered those buses were never seen again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point on the convoy, were you asked to get out of the bus and line up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I had already once changed buses during that trip. I had been with inmates from Trnopolje, together with my wife and children, and another man from my bus changed buses with me. He had a wife and a child with him, too. So our wives and children were the only ones on that bus. All the rest were men. And on our way across Mount Vlasic, at some point, the bus stopped near a creek. We didn't know why. On the right side of the road, so as to let the other buses pass by. At first, we were told to get out if we wanted to, because it was very hot the month of July. We were told we could go to the creek and drink some water if we liked. But when we got to the creek, or almost near the creek, we saw a lot of Serb soldiers. And nobody dared go any further. So for a while, we just sat there on the buses until we were eventually ordered by our police escorts to leave the buses, without exception, and to line up outside the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that mean to you? And from your knowledge of the camps, what did you think was about to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I stood in the line, just as everyone else. And at that moment, I thought I knew what was going to happen next with extreme clarity, from all my previous experience. I thought that we were going to be robbed again, beaten up, perhaps even something worse. Because that's the way that all the previous lineups I had seen ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: So as I said, we were standing there, lined up. And then one of the policemen said that -- actually, at one point, we were alone there. Our bus was the only one standing there. There was no one around. And while we were lined up, a trailer truck arrived and parked behind our bus. And then one of those policemen from our escort told the women to get on to that truck. My wife asked if we were allowed to take our things. And since she had a child, a baby less than a month old in her arms, while I was holding our other child, a four-year-old by the hand, she asked me to help her move her things. Actually, she asked for permission for me to help her move her things from the bus to the truck. And when I did so, she got on to the truck. The other man who had his wife and child with him did the same, and when we loaded everything, we got on and left. The truck departed leaving the bus behind together with all the people outside

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the men from the Trnopolje camp who were lined up in that line that you were able to get away from thanks to what your wife had had done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, there was a man who was a good friend of mine among the inmates. Himzo Mrkalj. While the majority of the rest were the men from Kozarac, whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the truck you were on continue on towards the front line, and then were you allowed to get out and did you walk to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The truck drove for a while, not long, and stopped again, pulled over at a clearing. And we were all ordered to get off. And the clearing was already full of people, very large number of people, who had already arrived on different trucks and buses which had got there before us so that we all continued again in the direction of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Himzo Mrkalj or any of the other men that you saw lined up at that last stop again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he or any of the other men that you remember, make it to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the people arrived past the front line, was there a concern among many of the people about their family members? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Only after we arrived in Travnik, while we were getting settled, finding accommodation, it was only then that we heard that ours was not the only bus that had been left there, that other men had been taken off other buses and trucks, two from one bus, three from another. And there were also two buses from Mount Vlasic which were also left there. And then people started making lists of their family members whom they believed to have been on those buses. And the list, when it was completed, contained more than 250 names, around that number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those thousands of people that you saw in Tukovi waiting to leave the territory, what was the ethnicity of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: All of them were Muslims, and a small number of Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were thousands, if you know, of Muslims and Croats wanting to leave the territory at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Because we no longer had any rights there. We no longer had the right to live, let alone own anything. Any day, somebody could come, confiscate your car, take away your house, shoot you, without ever being held responsible for it. So it was the only solution, the only way out, to go as far as away from there as possible, at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Your Honours. I'm far exceeding my estimate. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Even though it's an additional burden for Witness B, I don't believe it would be fair to start the cross-examination today. And therefore, we would kindly ask you to come back tomorrow in the afternoon for the cross-examination. For today, you're excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two small issues: There is a small mistake on the record at 18.22.02. There it says: "Exhibit S1B." It should read "S12B". Could this please be corrected. Thank you. And then I have to announce a decision of the Trial Chamber that it is ordered that a formal identification may take place next Friday. It's a burden of proof for the Office of the Prosecutor; and therefore, it is expected that the Office of the Prosecutor points out from possible persons, possibly some other inmates of the United Nations Detention Unit, to come. And I think this would be an idea - and I expect the comments from the parties to this - to come in the beginning of the hearing on Friday to this courtroom. And this would give all the participants, of course, especially the Bench, to see the immediate reactions of this witness. This is the best application of the principle of directness. Comments from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd rather see what can be arranged before I make any comments. I think the transportation and security people will have some problems. We'll try to deal with them, and then report to the Court what our comments are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I explained, on the basis of some domestic jurisdictions, I believe it's appropriate to have a number of five persons present. What are the comments of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We accept your proposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I hope we can overcome all obstacles, I'm aware of this, in order to come as close as possible to the truth. The trial stands adjourned. We resume tomorrow as indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
